slides.title: Hi, I’m Samarth
slides.body:
Product designer at Blink UX, an Mphasis company, in Austin. Five-plus years at Paytm, MakeMyTrip, Airtel Payments Bank and a few small teams.

A designer who's dream once started as a developer; and life (and AI) has got me full circle doing both now.

slides.title: Voyage
slides.lede: The design system behind $500M+ in enterprise deals
facts: Figma · Storybook · Claude Code · Chromatic · Dyad

slides.title: Great demos that never added up
slides.body:
I joined the pre-sales team, the group that builds demos for client proposals.

Every demo was built in a silo, so tied to one client that reusing it meant starting over. Nothing looked the same from one proposal to the next.

visual.html: Different clients, same patterns, rebuilt from scratch every time.

slides.title: Six months of research before the system took shape
slides.body: I interviewed 50+ designers about where demo work hurt, covering about 10 years of their work. I reviewed existing design systems to decide what to plug in, modify or build, and worked with marketing on the brand vision.

slides.title: A system first, demos second
slides.body: An MVP, six months building it out, then months of feedback sessions. The cost was time on a team that sells every week. Faster one-off demos would only have made more of the problem.

slides.title: One source of truth
slides.body:
The first version was the documentation every designer built from: brand philosophy, components in depth, usage guides and the reasoning behind each decision.

A central repository kept it up to date with standards for Android, iOS, web and accessibility.

slides.title: One parent, many children
slides.body:
Voyage is the parent. Teams build child systems that add or change components for their own work.

Weekly feedback sessions merge the useful changes back, so teams stay inside the system instead of working around it.

slides.title: What used to be a rebuild became a toggle
slides.body:
Sales kept asking for demos in the client's own look.

So I added fast switching between versions and themes: white-label by default, styled per client when a deal needs it.

slides.title: The system had to follow them
slides.body:
With AI, designers started building in Claude Code, Copilot, Claude Design and other tools.

Version two gave every component a contract, a context file and a stack-agnostic developer version, so any AI tool could build with it.

slides.title: Docs alone didn't stop the drift. Process did.
slides.body: AI reuses components first and writes what's missing into gaps.md. A designer decides which gaps are real. An admin approves what joins Voyage, and Chromatic checks it.

slides.title: What the system puts out
slides.body: Screens built with Voyage across products. One of them was made with the AI flow.

imgs.alt: Intelligence Hub home with AI nudges and assistant
Advisor dashboard with prospects, insights and North Star AI

slides.title: Faster at every version
slides.body: Clients this touched include Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, Charles Schwab, BlackRock, Corebridge and FedEx.

stats: in deals supported in one year
turnaround with Voyage AI, after −30% in v1

visual.html:
Docs don't stop drift. Process does.

Contracts and context files still drifted. Making reuse the only path and putting every gap in front of a person worked.

Let teams change the system

Child systems and weekly merges let teams adapt Voyage without leaving it.

img.alt: Paytm Chat on the Paytm homepage

slides.title: A team that was losing users
slides.body:
Competitors moved faster, and people were leaving for apps with quicker payments across banks and community features.

Paytm had tried chat two years earlier and dropped it.

visual.html: A native chat built around payments, to start conversations and bring people back to pay again.

slides.title: Users disagreed with the market
slides.body:
Competitors were adding payments into chats. Our users wanted chat added onto payments.

I studied WhatsApp, Hike, Instagram, Signal, Telegram, WeChat and Messages so chat would feel familiar, then ran a priority matrix with the business.

visual.html: “I come to Paytm to make payments, let me do that fast.”

slides.title: Two ways in. Pay first won.
slides.body:
With 100M users landing on it, we tested two launch flows.

Pay first halved the drop, so we shipped it. Competitors moved to a similar model within months.

slides.title: Every payment is a card
slides.body:
Paytm's design system had no chat patterns, so I built them from scratch.

I worked with compliance and payments on what each card could show: status, traceability and the icons the RBI allowed.

slides.title: Payment cards had to feel like chat, and pass compliance
slides.body: Payment cards in chat were a new direction for payments, with more traceability. They also had to cover every use case.

slides.title: One sticker, many stickers, and what shows while loading
slides.body: Stickers were our stand-out feature: upload a transparent GIF, get an animated sticker. I worked through rendering and every state with developers.

slides.title: PODS wasn’t built for chat
slides.body:
PODS, Paytm’s design system, was very new back then.

I added elements that fit it and carried the chat team’s vision, each with states, animations, size guidance and interaction guides. They stayed in the system as a new component category.

slides.title: People open the app to pay, not to chat
slides.body:
Other apps made you start a chat, then pay. Our statistics and interviews showed the reverse.

So paying someone connects to a chat or starts one. Within 2–3 months, the market was adapting too.

slides.title: Designing stickers with the launch in mind
slides.body:
I worked with business and marketing to see how they planned to advertise stickers, and we made custom stickers for launch.

Product screenshots, with marketing’s input, went into the collateral. That bridged a major gap in the team.

slides.title: People talk before they pay
slides.body:
Feedback after launch showed something the test missed. So I merged pay first with chat first.

With no payment yet, the pay button moves into the menu so people see where it went. An empty chat gets a big pay button.

slides.title: Each version lost fewer people
slides.body: Launched to 100M monthly users.

stats: left a chat without paying, chat first

visual.html:
Ask users before copying the market

The market said chat first. Our users said pay first, and the A/B test backed them.

A test winner isn't the end

Pay first won, but missed that people talk before paying. Listening after launch took the drop from 17% to 12%.

slides.title: Insider Vibes
slides.lede: 0 to 50,000 paying users in one month
facts: Figma · After Effects · Protopie · Rive · CleverTap

slides.title: The business disappeared in about three weeks
slides.body:
Insider’s entire business was offline events: ticketing and in-person shows. Then COVID happened.

We had six months of runway and no product. The mandate was simple to say and hard to do: build something people would pay for, fast, with no idea yet what that was.

stats: for the core business to vanish
of runway to find a new one

slides.title: Clubhouse and Google Meet each solved half of it
slides.body:
Clubhouse had the intimacy of audio-first rooms. Meet had scheduled, hosted structure. I compared them on five things.

Then user interviews and a value stream: what someone gets done when they come back a second time. I argued it out with the business until both lined up.

visual.html:
ClubhouseGoogle Meet
Audio vs videoLive audio roomsVideo conferencing
ExclusivityInvitation-only launchCorporate, closed use
CommunityRooms by shared interestCollaborative meetings
ModerationHost-controlled roomsAdmin controls
MonetisationCreator monetisationNone native
Insider VibesChat, audio and video in one: room-based communities with moderation and experience levels

slides.title: Three roles, three products inside one
slides.body: Most platforms design for participants and bolt on tooling for everyone else. We designed all three properly, because a community with weak moderation isn’t a community for long.

visual.html:
AdminCreate rooms, manage users, oversee content, set rules
ModeratorsSupport admins, monitor discussions, de-escalate conflict, report upward
ParticipantsParticipate, follow rules, build the community, personalise their profile

slides.title: A plug-and-play design system on a six-month runway
slides.body:
Every instinct said ship the fastest version and fix it later. I built the system flexible down to fonts, colours and components, knowing it would slow the first weeks.

Midway, engineering moved the stack from Angular to React. The interface barely felt it.

visual.html:
SlowerFirst few weeks

Building tokens and components before screens

Paid offAngular → React

Full stack rebuild midway, and the UI barely moved

slides.title: The design system underneath all of it
slides.body: Three fully designed roles, a joining flow that showed upfront what the platform could see and hear, and camera and mic controls front and centre. The system was translated into React components with the dev team so it could scale past v1 without a redesign.

slides.title: The expanding panel
slides.body: The bottom half is information-dense and some people want to live in it. Instead of a separate view, the top half shrinks as you scroll so the bottom can breathe. Removes a whole navigation step.

slides.title: Polls that interrupt just enough
slides.body: A bottom sheet on mobile, a small box top-right on desktop, animated in Protopie and Rive. Enough to answer, not enough to lose your place in the conversation.

slides.title: The room was worth coming back to
slides.body: The first number kept the company alive. The second is the one I care about: 62% coming back means the room itself was worth it, not just the novelty.

visual.html:
50,000+paying users in month one
62%return rate
Note from future Samarth

I set up CleverTap A/B tests and moved teams before seeing the results. Now I hand off a test with an owner and a date to check back. I’d also push harder to be in the room for stack decisions like Angular to React.
